item.title: PSI researcher receives 2.2 million for quantum research
item.description: Physicist Giacomo Sala wins a European funding of 2.3 million euros for the Q-GEOMSPIN project that combines spintronics and quantum geometry. Research that could revolutionise Swiss data storage.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Giacomo Sala (PSI) receives €2.3 million (~ CHF 2.2 million) from the European Research Council - Q-GEOMSPIN project: spintronics + quantum geometry for 5 years - Since the end of 2025, Switzerland has been fully associated with EU programmes
## Key facts - **What**: Starting ERC Grant for research in quantum spintronics - When: 3 September 2026 - Where: Paul Scherrer Institut (PSI), Villigen, Aargau - Who: Giacomo Sala, experimental physicist - Amount: €2.3 million (approx. CHF 2.2 million) - Duration: 5 years - Team: 2 PhD students + 1 postdoctoral researcher
Giacomo Sala, an experimental physicist at the Neutron and Muon Research Centre of the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Villigen, has won one of the most coveted grants from the European Research Council (ERC): a Starting Grant. The funding, amounting to 2.3 million euros — about CHF 2.2 million — will support his Q-GEOMSPIN project for the next five years. A victory that means a lot for Swiss research, especially in view of Switzerland's new full partnership with European research funding programmes, effective from the end of 2025.
What makes this initiative extraordinary? Sala combines two hitherto separate areas of research: spintronics, a discipline that has been consolidated for three decades, and quantum geometry, a young and still developing field. “As far as I know, so far no one has experimentally connected these two fields,” says Sala. ### Spintronics: from the laboratory to industrial application
Spintronics exploits the spin — the intrinsic rotation — of electrons to store and process information. The importance of this field was recognized with the 2007 Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded precisely for research in this area. However, in recent years, spintronics has presented a gap that is not yet fully understood: some theoretical physics studies suggest that certain spintronic phenomena can be predicted, understood, and controlled thanks to quantum geometry, and specifically thanks to a subfield of the latter: quantum metric.
Sala uses an intriguing analogy to explain the concept. Gravity causes the Earth to orbit the Sun. According to Albert Einstein, however, the correct explanation is not a simple 'attraction' but a curvature of space caused by the mass of the Sun. 'The same applies to electrons when they move through a solid,' explains Sala. Due to quantum metric, the momentum space curves. Electrons 'perceive' this phenomenon and are consequently deflected.
### Practical applications and economic impact
Research in the Q-GEOMSPIN project could pave the way for more efficient data storage systems. In the long term, the results could contribute to the development of more powerful spintronic memories (MRAM), computer processors that operate on the model of the brain, and new material properties. It is important to note that, with the exception of giant magnetoresistance, discovered in the 1980s and which soon multiplied the storage density of computer hard drives, commercial applications of spintronics have so far been rare. Sala's project could represent a significant turning point for the Swiss and European technology industry, with employment repercussions in the high-tech sector.
### PSI as a European hub for quantum research
The fact that Sala chose the Paul Scherrer Institut for his project is not coincidental. The PSI is one of the most important research centers in Europe, with unique infrastructures and research strategies aligned with national and European priorities. In the new 'Quantum Matter and Materials Center' (QMMC) of the PSI, the work of various research groups converges in the field of quantum matter and materials. Q-GEOMSPIN fits perfectly into this new research hub, strengthening Switzerland's position in international quantum research.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Advanced infrastructures and laboratory equipment
PSI provides Sala and his team with all the necessary structures to carry out research. The team will create and measure structures of a few micrometers in size, cooled to temperatures close to absolute zero (–273.15 degrees Celsius). For this purpose, PSI acquires, thanks to ERC funds, a special cryostat: a cooling device capable of generating strong magnetic fields. Inside it, an electric current will be passed through the sample and the deviation of the electrons will be measured. In this way, researchers are looking for non-linear effects, i.e., situations where small variations in voltage or magnetic field lead to large changes in measurement.
The team will have access to three excellent infrastructures: the Swiss Light Source (SLS), the PICO cleanroom (an advanced cleanroom managed by the nanotechnology group), and the Swiss Spallation Neutron Source (SINQ). These structures are unique in Europe and allow the characterization of materials at the nanometric level. The program includes the study of topological materials (solids that are insulators inside but conduct electricity on the surface), oxide compounds, and two-dimensional Van der Waals materials such as graphene.
### Career opportunities in Swiss quantum research
With ERC funding, Sala will be able to hire two PhD students and one postdoctoral researcher. Quantum research is one of the most dynamic and growing sectors of the Swiss economy. European funding programs, now fully accessible thanks to association by the end of 2025, offer concrete career opportunities for young researchers, PhD students, and postdocs throughout Switzerland. The sector is not limited to PSI: universities such as ETH Zurich, University of Geneva, University of Bern, and other Swiss universities are heavily investing in quantum research and the training of new talents.
The skills developed in research projects like Q-GEOMSPIN — from data analysis to nanotechnology, from experimental physics to materials engineering — are highly valued in the private sector, from microelectronics companies to industrial research laboratories. A career in Swiss quantum research offers stable employment prospects and internationally competitive salaries.
### How to access funding and research opportunities
If you are a student, researcher, or recent graduate interested in a career in Swiss research, the first step is to consult the [job opportunities in the research sector](nav:jobs) and learn about the [cost of living in Switzerland and the quality of research](nav:cost-of-living) in different regions. Universities and research centers regularly publish job postings for PhD, postdoc, and staff scientist positions.
The European Research Council regularly publishes calls for Starting Grants (up to 3.75 million euros), Consolidator Grants, and Advanced Grants. The terms and application procedures can be found on the official ERC website. Thanks to Switzerland's full association by the end of 2025, Swiss researchers can also apply directly, receiving funding without institutional intermediaries.
For those who want to delve into the economic impact of salaries in the research and public sector in Switzerland, compare opportunities in different cantons and regions, and plan their career path, the [Swiss salary calculator](nav:calculator) provides a detailed overview of salaries in the research and public sector.

item.description: The Conference of Governments of Western Switzerland meeting in Fribourg supports the package of agreements with the EU, underlining the importance for stable access to the continental market
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Western governments support Bilaterali III in Fribourg - 7 cantons gathered at the CGSO headquarters say yes to the package - Package under review by the Federal Parliament - Update agreements to protect access to the European market
## Key facts - **What**: Bilaterali III package between Switzerland and EU - When: Today's meeting of the Conference - Where: Fribourg - Who: Governments of 7 western cantons (Berne, Fribourg, Geneva, Jura, Neuchâtel, Vaud, Valais) - Status: Under review by the Federal Parliament - Importance: Ensure long-term access to the continental market for Swiss companies
The Conference of the Governments of Western Switzerland (CGSO) gathered today in Fribourg the representatives of seven cantons—Berne, Fribourg, Geneva, Jura, Neuchâtel, Vaud and Valais—to express full support for the package of agreements between the Confederation and the European Union, known as Bilaterali III. The decision is relevant because the package is currently under review by the Federal Parliament and is considered essential to ensure Swiss companies stable access to the continental market.
### The origin of the stalemate: from 2021 to the blocking of updates
In 2021, Switzerland abandoned the negotiations on the institutional framework agreement with the EU. Since then, Brussels has refused to update several market access agreements, blocking the evolution of European legislation in the affected sectors. This situation exposes Swiss companies—in particular SMEs—to complicated procedures and additional costs to operate within the Union.
According to the CGSO, the Bilaterali III package is the concrete solution to this stalemate. It provides an official mechanism to resolve disputes between Bern and Brussels and ensures the continuation of Swiss participation in European programs such as Horizon Europe. The western cantonal governments emphasize the importance of regularly updating the agreements, not as an isolated event but as a structural process of adaptation to the continuously evolving European legislation. ### The concrete impact on Swiss companies
The lack of updated agreements directly affects Swiss companies exporting to the EU. Currently, a Swiss SME faces administrative procedures that diverge from European legislation: duplication of certifications, additional audits, longer customs clearance times. For a small to medium-sized company, these costs are significant in relation to overall turnover and operational margins.
The dispute resolution mechanism included in the Bilaterali III package is a crucial novelty compared to the status quo. So far, disputes between Bern and Brussels have been resolved slowly or not at all, blocking entire sectors and creating prolonged normative uncertainty. A defined mechanism would accelerate disputes and significantly reduce the business risk for Swiss exporters.
### Research, innovation, and global competitiveness
Access to European research programs such as Horizon Europe is not a mere administrative detail: Swiss universities, research centers, and innovative startups depend on these funds to remain competitive in the international landscape. The absence of regular participation would result in the loss of critical international collaborations, reduced access to R&D funds, and the gradual marginalization of Swiss research in the European context.
The renewal of the Bilaterali III therefore concerns not only traditional industry and commerce but the entire Swiss innovation ecosystem. The position of the CGSO is strategic: these seven cantons represent open economies, with strong exporters and established multinationals. The endorsement of the Conference signals clear political consensus among the cantonal administrations, providing a solid basis for parliamentary approval.

If you manage a Swiss company that exports to the EU or depends on European suppliers, the Bilaterali III package directly affects your competitiveness and strategic planning. Here are the operational steps to monitor and prepare.
**Monitor parliamentary timelines**: The package is under review by the Federal Parliament. You can follow the process by consulting the official communications of the Federal Council on admin.ch or the parliamentary messages on parlament.ch. Approval timelines will be publicly announced well in advance, allowing for adequate business planning.
Assess the specific impact on your sector: Not all sectors are affected equally. Manufacturing, chemical, pharmaceutical industries, and financial services will benefit most from regulatory stability. A meeting with a commercial consultant or your Swiss industry association can clarify the specific implications for your business.
Plan gradual regulatory transitions: If you currently use procedures that are not updated to EU standards, the package will mark a transition towards progressive alignment. Gather documentation on current regulatory gaps and plan compliance investments before the official entry into force.

item.description: Swiss GDP +1.5% in Q2 2026. SECO slows down on boom, but enlarged growth and domestic demand recovers. Annual forecasts under review in two weeks.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Swiss GDP +1.5% in Q2 2026 compared to Q1 - SECO: not a boom, but growth with a broad sectoral base - Annual GDP forecast (0.9%) could rise in upcoming estimates
## Key facts - **What**: Stronger-than-expected quarterly GDP growth, driven by the chemical-pharmaceutical sector - When: Second quarter 2026 - Where: Switzerland (data from the Swiss State Secretariat for Economy) - Who: SECO with economic cycle manager Felicitas Kemeny - Amount: +1.5% q-o-q; annual GDP estimate 0.9% (under review) - Leading sector: Chemical-pharmaceutical industry - Next decision: Within two weeks of the announcement
The strong growth recorded by the Swiss economy in the second quarter of 2026, with a 1.5% increase compared to the previous three months, shines a spotlight on the national economic situation. However, the Swiss State Secretariat for Economy (SECO) advises a measured assessment. Felicitas Kemeny, head of the economic cycle section at SECO, is clear: this does not represent a boom in the economy.
### Federal institution's caution
The main driver of the expansion has been the chemical-pharmaceutical industry, a historic pillar of the Swiss economy. Yet, a crucial question remains: is this truly sustainable growth, or are we simply seeing the effects of anticipation or recovery after the declines in previous months? Kemeny has not provided a definitive answer, but caution is clearly evident in the SECO's statement.
What reassures observers is the broad base of the recovery. Added value has increased in numerous other sectors beyond the chemical-pharmaceutical industry. More importantly, internal demand — household spending and private investment — has started to rise again after a weak start to the year, signaling that the dynamism is not concentrated in a single economic niche.
### Forecasts in limbo for 2026
So far, SECO economists had forecast a gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 0.9% for the entire year 2026. However, the magnitude of the quarterly surprise opens up a scenario of upward revision. SECO will communicate the new official projection within two weeks. Kemeny has openly acknowledged that "the possibility of an upward revision of the estimates is concrete".
More optimistic than Kemeny is Thomas Gitzel, chief economist at VP Bank. "This year, the Swiss economy is going quite well", declares Gitzel in a comment on the data. The expert attributes the momentum to a "surprising recovery" in European industry at this time, a trend that also benefits Swiss exporters. However, Gitzel also warns: although the strong GDP increase in Q2 is positive, "it is unlikely to be repeated with the same intensity in the short term"; growth rates will nevertheless remain "robust". ### What do these data mean for those working in Switzerland
A PIL growth that extends beyond the chemical-pharmaceutical sector has concrete reflections on the labor market and available income. When more economic sectors simultaneously record increases in added value and domestic demand rises, companies tend to invest more and hire new personnel. Switzerland, with a historically low unemployment rate, could see a further decline.
This means upward pressure on wages, particularly in secondary sectors such as construction, logistics, and commerce, which traditionally suffer less from the volatility of high-tech segments but directly benefit from the increase in consumption and private investment. An economy that grows with a broad base, as emphasized by Kemeny, is a sign that job opportunities are distributed beyond the traditional Swiss excellence niches.
### Implications for federal and cantonal taxation
Sustained economic growth increases the gross taxable income of families and employers, thereby increasing federal (direct federal tax) and cantonal revenues. Although this does not immediately result in changes in national tax rates, cantonal and municipal governments may find more room for maneuver in the 2027 and subsequent budgets.
On the other hand, growth that does not translate into structural inflation — as suggested by Kemeny's caution regarding the sustainability of rates — limits the pressure on LAMal premiums (mandatory sickness insurance). Currently, Swiss premiumists are affected by moderate annual increases; an economy that grows without overheating is the preferred scenario for federal authorities.
### What to monitor in the coming weeks
Analysts from SECO and private sector observe two critical variables: the durability of the contribution from domestic demand and the stability of the chemical-pharmaceutical sector relative to global cycles. If domestic demand does not consolidate in the following quarters, the PIL may return to annual rates around 0.9%. If, however, the recovery extends, the revision of forecasts could lead SECO to estimate an annual expansion of 1.2–1.5%.
Such a scenario would change the risk profile for real wages (income net of inflation). In a context of robust growth without rampant inflation, real wages are likely to rise, benefiting particularly employed workers in sectors driven by new demand for goods and services.

Swiss economic growth data is regularly released by SECO, which publishes seasonal economic projections on a quarterly basis. The next revision of the annual growth estimates for 2026 is expected within two weeks of the original Q2 data release, according to Felicitas Kemeny.
For those who want to monitor the national economy's performance — workers, employers, and border workers looking for occupational opportunities — it is useful to regularly consult the official SECO website (seco.admin.ch), where economic projections, economic situation press releases, and detailed data by sector are published. This practice allows for anticipating possible changes in the labor market and income scenarios.
### Important deadlines and upcoming decisions
The official SECO revision communication will take place by the first weekend of September 2026. An estimated growth of 1.2–1.5% would significantly change the available resources for federal and cantonal budgets, potentially influencing decisions on cantonal tax rates, funding for employment policies, and, in some cantons, revisions of the minimum wage.
For new workers or those renegotiating contracts, a growing economy is a strength: there is a higher probability of salary increases and better occupational conditions. Finally, for those seeking new occupational opportunities, robust economic growth is usually accompanied by a labor market recovery: [regularly consulting national job announcement portals](/nav:jobs) is a winning strategy to capitalize on expansion phases like the current one.

item.description: UBS revises Swiss GDP 2026 from +0.7% to +1.8%. Inflation August 0.8%, estimates 2026-2027 stable at 0.6%. What changes for wages and cost of living.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief
- UBS revises upwards: GDP 2026 from +0.7% to +1.8% excluding sports - August inflation 0.8%, 2026-2027 estimates stable at 0.6% - Swiss economic prospects improve significantly
## Key facts
- **What**: UBS raises Swiss economic growth forecasts - When: Today, after SECO Q2 GDP data - Where: Switzerland - Who: UBS (largest Swiss bank), SECO, Federal Statistical Office (FSO) - Amount: GDP +1.8% versus previous +0.7%; +2.2% with sporting events - Inflation: 0.8% in August; 0.6% expected 2026-2027
---
Zurich — UBS significantly revises upwards its forecasts for Swiss economic growth. The largest Swiss bank predicts that gross domestic product (GDP) will increase by 1.8% this year, compared to the previously estimated +0.7%. Including sports, the figure will reach +2.2%.
The announcement comes at a time of renewed confidence in the national economic cycle. The revision emerges from the analysis titled "Economic prospects improve significantly" released today by UBS following the publication of Q2 GDP data by the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO). The Q2 numbers exceeded expectations, prompting the bank's analysts to recalibrate their projections upwards.
### 2027 growth slightly higher
The forecast for 2027 is also increased, albeit modestly. The estimate rises from the previous +1.4% to +1.5%. A modest but significant increase in the context of an economy accelerating compared to predictions from a few months ago.
On the price front, today's inflation data released by the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) surprised UBS analysts: in August, inflation reached 0.8%. Despite this figure, the institute's experts do not foresee a fundamental change in price dynamics. Therefore, they maintain the estimate of a 0.6% increase for both 2026 and 2027. This inflation stability represents a positive element in the context of stronger-than-expected economic growth. The renewed prospects reflect a more resilient Swiss economy than initially expected, with accelerations that could have significant implications for the labor market, consumption, and federal and cantonal budget dynamics. ## What changes for Swiss residents
The upward correction of growth is not an economic abstraction, but a signal that can affect various aspects of the daily life of those residing in Switzerland. Stronger GDP growth generally goes hand in hand with a more dynamic labor market, with companies investing and hiring. In the Swiss context, where the unemployment rate is already low, an additional 0.8 percentage points of growth compared to previous estimates could translate into more competitive salaries and greater professional advancement opportunities.
At the same time, the expected inflation stability — 0.6% annually in 2026 and 2027 — represents a guarantee for purchasing power. While economic growth tends to push prices up, Swiss monetary authorities and economic actors are aiming for lasting moderation. This balance is crucial for those who depend on fixed incomes or subsidies: rents, health insurance premiums (LAMal/KVG), food, and services should remain on a predictable trajectory, without sudden shocks.
### Implications for savings and investments
For those with financial portfolios, the improvement in economic prospects can mean more favorable conditions in the markets. An expected growth of 1.8% annually — or 2.2% if the effects of major sporting events are considered — suggests that listed companies, pension funds, and investment instruments linked to the economic cycle could benefit from stronger economic fundamentals. It is not a guarantee, but a less uncertain context compared to previous projections.
It is still relevant to monitor [cost of living in your canton](nav:cost-of-living): stronger economic growth does not mean that prices remain static. Rents and services can vary by region. Even those contributing to the third pillar (3a) for pension choices might consider repositioning in light of the improved prospects. Stronger economic growth generally supports medium-term returns, although geopolitical risks remain ever-present.

## In a nutshell - mfe criticizes the TARDOC for not re-evaluating family medicine - Increasing outpatient costs, family medicine devalued in some cantons - Risk of removing young doctors from primary care in Switzerland
## Key facts - **What**: Criticism of the TARDOC medical tariff by Mfe - When: Communication issued by mfe (date not specified in the source) - Where: Zurich (MFE headquarters), Swiss health system - Who: Family and children's doctors Switzerland (MFE), Monika Reber and Sébastien Jotterand, co-chairs - Problem: Increased outpatient costs without re-evaluation of family medicine
The Swiss Family and Children's Medical Association (Mfe) has issued a statement critical of the TARDOC, the new medical tariff. According to the association, the introduction of this tool has not materialized the revaluation of family medicine, a goal required by every political and health party.
On the contrary, the observed picture reveals a worrying trend. The TARDOC system has led to a considerable increase in overall costs in the outpatient sector, while family medicine has even suffered a devaluation in some cantons. The only notable exception: pediatricians and general practitioners register a slight improvement in their rates.
### The persistent tariff imbalance
"Overall, the TARDOC system shows a considerable increase ### The impact on young doctors and the healthcare system
The problem goes beyond the simple economic issue. According to mfe, the tariff evolution sends a decidedly negative message to young doctors who are considering which specialty to choose. If family medicine remains economically less attractive than other specialties, with equal training and clinical responsibility, the concrete risk is that an entire generation of professionals will move away from it.
"A tariff system that disadvantages primary care so blatantly worsens the shortage of family doctors instead of combating it," says Sébastien Jotterand, co-president of the association. The shortage of family doctors is already a critical reality in many Swiss regions. To better understand how your access to primary care is ensured by the healthcare system, you can [consult the LAMal system guide](nav:health). Further professional disincentives could drastically worsen access to services for resident citizens.
### mfe's proposal: targeted, not linear corrections
mfe recognizes that, due to the general increase in costs, some tariff adjustments are inevitable to meet the cost-neutrality requirements set by the Federal Council. However, the association firmly opposes a linear devaluation that affects all medical specialties equally.
The association instead proposes differentiated and targeted tariff corrections in sectors where tariffs are truly inadequate. Specifically:
- Areas with excessive time allocations - Specialties where infrastructure and personnel costs have been underestimated
This calibrated strategy should have protected family medicine from further reductions, concentrating adjustments only where effectively necessary and justified by cost data.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How TARDOC influences the Swiss healthcare system
TARDOC is the reference tariff for outpatient medical services in Switzerland. The established rates directly impact the costs managed by health insurance funds, which in turn influence the premiums of mandatory health insurance (LAMal/KVG) that every resident is required to subscribe to. When overall outpatient costs increase, health insurance funds commonly pass on these increases to citizens through premium hikes.
The current situation therefore represents a multi-level challenge: on one hand, the overall costs of outpatient care have risen, which could impact premiums for all insured individuals; on the other hand, family medicine — which serves as the gateway to the system for most patients — loses economic appeal, risking a shortage of professionals that would reduce supply and lengthen waiting times.
### Next developments and monitoring
mfe's criticisms open a broader discussion on how the Federal Council intends to address the cost-neutrality constraints without compromising the quality and accessibility of primary care. The association will continue to urge the government to review linear tariff adjustments and opt for a more differentiated and sustainable strategy.
Residents of Switzerland can follow the evolution of the debate by monitoring the official communications of the Federal Council and professional medical associations. In the event of further tariff adjustments, communications will primarily occur through the official channels of the federal administration.

item.description: Cross-cutting motion to the Federal Council to prevent childcare abuse. The government stalls and promises a report by the end of 2027.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - National councillor calls for a national blacklist for kindergarten educators - Model for the list already exists for school teachers - Federal Council delays: report expected by the end of 2027 - Motion signed across party lines by deputies from all parties
## Key facts - **Who**: Nina Fehr Düsel (SVP/ZH), Federal Council, Swiss Parliament - What: Motion to establish a national blacklist for kindergarten staff involved in sexual abuse - When: Motion submitted; government report by the end of 2027 - Where: Bern, at the federal level - Why: Prevent educators with a history of abuse from moving between cantons without trace
Cases of sexual abuse in kindergartens have prompted Parliament to react. National Councillor Nina Fehr Düsel (SVP/Zurich) has submitted a motion asking the Federal Council to establish a national blacklist for staff in these childcare facilities, modeled after the existing list for schools.
The Swiss Conference of Cantonal Ministers of Education (EDK) already maintains a list of individuals who have had their teaching license revoked due to criminal offenses, including sexual crimes. The purpose is to prevent them from working in other cantons.
### The regulatory void in kindergartens
Educators in childcare facilities do not have a similar tool. According to Fehr Düsel, a centralized list would be even more important in kindergartens: it would prevent professionals who have committed abuse from moving to another canton without trace to find new employment. Schools are promptly informed of any issues in case of multiple employments; kindergartens are not.
The motion received cross-party support from deputies of all parties, indicating widespread consensus on the issue. However, in its recently published response, the Federal Council decided to delay and rejected the motion.
The government explained that it is preparing a comprehensive report on sexual abuse committed against minors. The investigation will examine the issue in various socialization contexts, particularly in out-of-home childcare facilities, and will also assess the possibility of creating blacklists. The report will be presented by the end of 2027 at the latest.
The executive asks to wait for the results of this report before taking concrete measures. However, political pressure continues to grow: the cross-party signature of the motion suggests that the government may need to speed up the process. ### Current system: differences between schools and daycare centers
The protection of minors in Swiss educational institutions relies on established tools. The CDPE coordinates nationally the data on teachers who have lost their certification for disciplinary reasons, including sexual offenses. This system allows schools to verify the background of candidates and to communicate between Cantons to prevent the transfer of unfit personnel.
For daycare centers and childcare facilities, there is no equivalent. Verification procedures vary from Canton to Canton, and there is no national coordination. An educator who has committed abuse in one Canton could theoretically find work in another, unless the victim also files a complaint there — a scenario that exposes children to significant risks. If you are a parent looking for information on certified childcare facilities in your Canton, it is useful to delve into local regulations.
### Why the pressure is growing
The Fehr Düsel motion has been signed by parliamentarians from the right, center, left, and greens. This cross-party consensus reflects a genuine and widespread concern for the safety of childcare facilities. The Parliament, in short, has sent a clear message: the issue is not divisive, but urgent.
The Federal Council cannot easily ignore a motion so widely supported, even if it has formally rejected it. It is likely that the 2027 deadline for the report on sexual abuse will provide the opportunity to adopt concrete measures, including the creation of a national blacklist.
### What would change for the Cantons and facilities
A national blacklist would have significant administrative implications. Each Canton is responsible for the authorization and supervision of daycare centers within its territory. A centralized list would require coordination between the cantonal authorities (probably through the CDPE or a federal agency), standardized procedures for reporting abuse cases, guaranteed access to childcare facilities, and protection of personal data for those under investigation. Implementation is not immediate: it requires a legal basis, clear governance, and investments in IT infrastructure. The delay in the federal response probably reflects this complexity.

Anyone who is a parent or educator in Switzerland should not wait passively for the government report in 2027. Today it is possible to take concrete actions:
Parents. Check if your Canton has a system of certificates of good conduct ("Federal Certificate of Good Conduct") for kindergarten staff. Some Cantons already require it when signing the contract; others do not. Ask the facility directly which checks have been carried out on the background of the staff. You can contact the competent cantonal office (normally the coordination office of the reception facilities or an educational office) to report concerns. For issues related to [parental leave and family rights](nav:parental-leave), many cantonal offices offer updated guidelines.
Reception facilities. If you are managers of a kindergarten, it is advisable to adopt, from now on, stricter staff verification procedures, even in advance of national legislation. Check compliance with current cantonal laws and consider registering staff with voluntary certification systems.
Monitoring. The federal report on sexual abuse, expected by the end of December 2027, will be a milestone. It must contain concrete recommendations on the blacklist and other prevention measures. It is likely that a federal consultation with the Cantons will follow before a possible legislative change.
### Where to find information
To deepen the cantonal regulations on kindergartens, consult the competent authority of your Canton. The Federal Council will publish the report on the website of the Federal Chancellery. Interested parties (Cantons, parents' associations, educators' organizations) will have a say in the subsequent consultation.
Next step. Monitor the announcements of the Federal Council for the report expected by December 31, 2027. In the meantime, if you are involved in the world of kindergartens, check the status of the legislation in your Canton and adopt the protection measures available today. item.title: Swiss economy accelerates, GDP +1.5% in 2026
item.description: SECO confirms strong growth in Q2 2026 with GDP +1.5%. Manufacturing and chemical-pharmaceutical industries are driving the Swiss economic recovery.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Swiss economy growing: GDP +1.5% in Q2 2026 confirmed by SECO - Industry leading: +3.9% (manufacturing +4.5%, chemical +10.5%) - Goods exports +5.5%, domestic demand recovers after weak start to the year
## Key facts - **What**: SECO press release on quarterly economic growth - When: Q2 2026 (confirmed 3 September 2026) - Where: Switzerland (national level) - Who: State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) - GDP Q2 vs Q1: +1.5% (vs +0.5% in the first quarter of 2026) - Strongest sector: Chemical-pharmaceutical industry (+10.5%) - 2026 forecasts: between +0.9% and +1.3% (SECO, OECD, SNB, KOF, UBS, Economiesuisse)
The State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) has confirmed the first estimate released in mid-August: the Swiss economy in the second quarter of 2026 showed strong growth. Gross domestic product rose by 1.5% compared to the previous three months, against the +0.5% observed in the first part of the year. According to federal experts, the largest contribution came from the chemical-pharmaceutical industry. However, value creation also increased in numerous other sectors. After a subdued start to the year, domestic demand returned to growth.
### Industry and exports: the true drivers of recovery
In sector detail, industry recorded a +3.9%, with a decisive contribution from the manufacturing sector (+4.5%). After some previous quarters that were partly weak and negative, the chemical-pharmaceutical segment soared (+10.5%), thanks in part to the increase in exports. Overall, goods exports rose by 5.5%. These figures testify to the ability of the most strategic sectors of the Swiss economy to maintain competitiveness in global markets. The dynamics of exports are particularly relevant in an international context that is still uncertain, where Swiss manufacturing has managed to defend and expand its market shares.
### Services: moderate but broad-based growth
Although moderate, the development of the services sector (+0.7%) was broad-based according to SECO experts. It was contributed to by the transport sector (+1.9%), the communications sector (+1.1%), as well as financial services (+1.9%). Service exports also increased (+1.6%). This widespread growth in services underscores that the recovery is not concentrated in a few sectors, but rather reflects a cross-sectional recovery of the economy. The growth of the financial sector is significant for a country like Switzerland, where this sector represents a fundamental structural element.
After the previous subdued quarter, final domestic demand growth rose to historical average levels (+0.5%). All major components played their part. Private consumption spending recorded a moderate increase (+0.3%): in particular, spending on health, food products, housing and catering increased; less was spent on transport, leisure and culture.
In line with the development of consumption, trade (+0.8%) recovered compared to the January-March period, characterized by a negative trend. In the retail sector (+1.2%), real turnover increased mainly in the food sector. The hotel and catering sector also made progress (+1.4%), thanks to the increase in overnight stays by national guests. Public administration consumption also rose (+0.4%) and investments (+0.7% in construction, +0.8% in equipment goods). In line with the overall growth in domestic demand, imports also increased (+2.2%). ### Employment dynamics: expanding sectors The economic growth of the second quarter of 2026 directly translates into job opportunities. The sectors that have recorded the best performances — industry, chemical-pharmaceutical, transport, finance — are typically sectors with a high density of qualified employment. When manufacturing grows by 4.5% and the chemical-pharmaceutical segment by 10.5%, demand for new resources is created: engineers, technicians, production specialists, administrative personnel. The Swiss labor market, already characterized by very low unemployment, finds itself in an even more favorable position. For dependent workers, the dynamic is positive. Expanding sectors offer greater job stability and, traditionally, wider spaces for salary negotiation. The 5.5% growth in merchandise exports creates positive ripple effects on supplier companies, sub-suppliers, and logistics.
### Recovery of domestic demand: implications for income and consumption After a weak start to the year (GDP +0.5% in Q1), the recovery of domestic demand in Q2 (+0.5%) signals that consumers and businesses are regaining confidence. When economic confidence improves, real wages — those adjusted for inflation — tend to maintain or improve purchasing power. The increase in private consumption (+0.3%), although moderate, is widespread: health, food, housing, catering record growth. This means that Swiss families have stable incomes and are willing to spend. The fact that retail trade grows by 1.2%, especially in the food sector, suggests solidity in the income base of household economies. When consumption grows, the latest available data for 2025 shows that the overall GDP for the year stood at +1.2% compared to the previous year, with Q4 2025 growing (+0.2%) after a negative Q3 (-0.4%).
### Official forecasts and scenarios for 2026 Based on this Q2 performance, the main Swiss authorities (SECO, OECD, Swiss National Bank, KOF, Economiesuisse, UBS, and others) forecast a GDP increase of between 0.9% and 1.3% for the entire year 2026. This is a scenario of moderate but positive growth. If the forecasts materialize, 2026 would be a year of consolidation compared to the uncertainties of 2025. Swiss imports in Q2 rose by 2.2%, signaling that internal growth fuels demand for foreign goods, a typical sign of an expansionary phase. The Swiss economy is not accelerating towards a boom but maintains a stable and widespread growth path.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How this growth affects you: wages, employment, investments
For those living and working in Switzerland, economic growth has concrete implications for paychecks, job stability, and career prospects. Driving sectors such as industry, chemical-pharmaceutical, finance, and transport represent a significant share of Swiss GDP. When these sectors accelerate, they hire additional staff and increase profitability margins — factors that traditionally favor more favorable wage negotiations in collective labor agreements (CLA). Switzerland has a structurally low unemployment rate (between 1% and 2%). During periods of robust economic growth, this value tends to decrease further, creating a relative shortage of talent and increased competition among employers to attract the best professionals. In this context, real wages (adjusted for inflation) have room for growth.
### Pension and financial planning
Solid economic growth also has indirect implications for pensions and investments. When the economy grows at the expected rate (0.9%-1.3% in 2026), corporate profits tend to rise, along with contributions to pension funds (LPP/BVG). Private sector pension funds, in fact, benefit from investment returns and the solidity of the participating companies. Moreover, periods of economic growth offer better opportunities for those wishing to invest in the [third pillar (3a)](nav:pillar3) or savings instruments, as income stability allows for more predictable savings plans.
### What to do now: consult federal tools
If you are employed in Switzerland, this positive economic dynamic does not require immediate action, but it is useful to know:
1. Check your salary position: consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to assess whether your income is in line with current federal and cantonal parameters. Robust economic growth creates negotiation spaces in CLAs — if your company reports growing profits, now is the right time to discuss raises.
2. Check LPP contributions: economic growth improves the fundamentals of pension funds. Ask your employer or pension fund for the expected returns of your fund in 2026. If they are above 3-4%, your pension assets are consolidated.
3. Plan your savings: with stable incomes and economic growth, now is the right time for voluntary contributions to the [third pillar (3a)](nav:pillar3) or to subscribe to additional protections via [companies and insurers](nav:companies).
Stay updated on Swiss economic growth and employment impacts in your sector: consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to verify your salary position against federal and cantonal parameters.

item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Regular gasoline reaches 2.10 CHF, diesel 2.26 CHF according to TCS - Prices close to the peak of August 20, +20-26% since February 2024 - Cause: Middle East conflict and water scarcity on the Rhine
## Key facts - **What**: Fuel prices rise to annual highs - When: Today according to TCS, previous peak on August 20, 2024 - Where: Switzerland (fuel stations) - Who: Touring Club Switzerland (TCS) - Regular gasoline: 2.10 CHF/liter - Diesel: 2.26 CHF/liter - Increase: +20-26% since late February 2024
The cost of fuel at the pump is rising again and is now almost at the annual high. According to the Touring Club Switzerland (TCS), the conflict in the Middle East and logistical difficulties on the Rhine are putting pressure on international fuel supplies to the Confederation. Today's data shows that the situation has returned to critical levels for those managing a car travel budget.
Regular unleaded gasoline averages 2.10 francs per liter, while the 98 version reaches 2.12 francs. Diesel, on the other hand, rises to 2.26 francs. The values are just one cent below the peaks reached on August 20, when prices hit the annual high up to that point. Since the start of the war in Iran, which broke out at the end of February, fuel prices have risen between 20 and 26 percent. A significant increase that reflects the volatility of international markets and the direct impact of geopolitics on consumer prices in Switzerland.
### How fuel prices are determined in Switzerland
This new surge is mainly explained by the international context. According to TCS experts, the pump price in Switzerland is traditionally linked to three main variables: the trend of crude oil prices on the Rotterdam exchange, the exchange rate of the US dollar against the Swiss franc, and the costs of river transport on the Rhine. The latter factor adds an additional critical element particularly relevant today.
The exceptional water scarcity affecting the major European river this period has drastically reduced the cargo capacity of barges, essential elements for transporting fuels inland. This reduction in logistics capacity has caused transport tariffs for fuel imports to the Confederation to soar, further worsening the final cost picture. For Swiss fuel importers and station managers, this means direct additional costs that inevitably pass on to end consumers. ### Structural damage to global refining capacity
This is compounded by a deeper structural damage that goes beyond mere logistical factors: global refining capacity has been severely compromised by both the conflict in Ukraine and that in Iran. These two parallel conflicts have drastically reduced the supply of finished products on the global market, creating a bottleneck that affects all importing countries, including Switzerland.
When global refining capacity decreases, the supply of finished fuels becomes scarcer compared to demand. This basic imbalance automatically translates into higher prices for those importing these products. Switzerland, completely dependent on fuel imports and without its own refineries, is particularly affected by this phenomenon. The Rhine, already under pressure due to water scarcity, represents an additional bottleneck in the European logistics chain that further amplifies the impact on final costs.
### Comparison with the 2022 peaks: the historical context
A note of relief for Swiss drivers: current prices remain lower than the staggering levels reached after the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. At that time, the price of a liter of 95-octane gasoline exceeded the threshold of 2.30 francs, a value considerably higher than the current 2.10 francs. The difference of 20 centimes may seem modest, but on an annual basis, it represents a significant saving for those who regularly use the car.
However, the upward trend remains evident and concerning for those managing mobility budgets. TCS experts warn that the situation remains fluid and vulnerable. With geopolitical tensions in the Middle East far from resolved and logistical difficulties on the Rhine set to continue at least until the river's water conditions improve, the risk of further price increases in the coming weeks remains concrete and significant.

For those who commute daily by car in Switzerland, these price increases have a direct and measurable impact on their monthly budget. An increase of just over 20 cents per liter for diesel and gasoline is not trivial when multiplied by the average annual consumption of a vehicle. Considering a car with an average consumption of 6.5 liters per 100 kilometers and an annual mileage of 15,000 kilometers, approximately 975 liters are consumed each year.
With current prices, the annual fuel cost for this vehicle amounts to around 2,100 francs, based on an average of 2.16 francs per liter for both gasoline and diesel. If this same car had remained at the prices of late February (before the recent price hikes), the annual cost would have been about 23% lower, approximately 1,650 francs. The difference translates to an additional annual expense of about 450 francs for fuel alone due to the recent price increase. For those who work or have regular trips to Switzerland, this is a figure that directly affects their net budget profitability.
### Practical strategies and monitoring
While it is not possible to directly influence international prices and geopolitical conflicts, there are practical strategies to mitigate the impact. Firstly, comparing prices between different fuel stations in your area can make a concrete difference: variations between different pumps can easily reach several cents per liter, which means dozens of francs saved annually. Secondly, optimizing routes and driving times to reduce overall consumption remains effective.

The Federal Department of Finance (FDF) published on 3 September a new working document dedicated to the demographic dynamics of the country. The text, entitled 'Niedrige Geburtenraten: Eine finanzpolitische Einordnung', analyzes in depth the phenomenon of the decline in birth rates, which in Switzerland has reached the lowest level ever recorded. This trend is not just a social change but constitutes a structural challenge for the entire national economic system. The contraction in the number of births, in fact, triggers a mechanism that slows down the growth of the active population, progressively reducing the available workforce to support the social security system. The FDF report highlights how the persistence of these low birth rates inevitably accelerates the demographic aging of the Swiss population. This demographic transition process has direct and measurable impacts on public finances, putting long-term budgets under pressure. The objective of the document is to provide an analytical basis to understand the deep causes of this evolution and to outline possible approaches for a forward-looking economic and financial policy, capable of addressing the consequences of a changing demography. ## In short
 - Q2 2026 GDP: +1.5% excluding sporting events, stronger than Q3 2021
 - Chemical-pharmaceutical industry grows by 10.5% with export boom
 - Domestic demand returns to historical levels (+0.5%) after a weak first quarter
 - Retail trade and hotel industry recovering (+1.2% and +1.4%)

 ## Key Facts
 - **What**: Swiss quarterly gross domestic product growth
 - When: Q2 2026 (data released on September 3, 2026)
 - Where: Switzerland
 - Who: SECO (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) with data from the FSO (Federal Statistical Office)
 - Total GDP: +1.5% excluding sporting events vs. 0.5% in the previous quarter
 - Leading sector: Chemical-pharmaceutical industry +10.5%
 - Merchandise exports: +5.5% overall
 - Domestic demand: +0.5% after a weak previous quarter

 Switzerland’s economy is picking up pace after slowing in the first half of the year. Gross domestic product (GDP), excluding sporting events, grew by 1.5% in the second quarter of 2026, the strongest growth since the third quarter of 2021. SECO released the data on September 3, 2026. After 0.5% in the first quarter, the rebound is broad-based and supported by multiple sectors.

 The chemical-pharmaceutical industry was the main driver of growth, climbing the rankings with a 10.5 percent gain thanks to exponential increases in exports and turnover. This is a significant figure for a country where this sector has a significant impact. ### What does it mean for Swiss economy in the medium term
The rebound in Q2 GDP represents a positive signal for employment, business confidence, and investments in the coming quarter. The recovery in domestic demand is particularly important as it suggests that private consumption is returning to growth after a sluggish start to the year. For those working in Switzerland, a broad-based GDP growth reduces the risk of recession and supports business decisions to maintain or expand their workforce.
Investments have provided further positive impulses. Investments in construction registered +0.7%, although residential construction has declined slightly, offset by growth in other construction and civil engineering. Investments in capital goods have risen by 0.8%, driven by other vehicles and research & development, although a decline in IT and machinery investments has partially offset the overall recovery. In line with the growth in domestic demand, imports have increased by 2.2%, reflecting both the need for raw materials and semi-finished goods for export production and the rise in consumption.
### Winning sectors and grey areas
The chemical-pharmaceutical industry represents a significant share of the Swiss economy: a +10.5% in a single quarter is a significant figure for the balance of trade. However, the data for the manufacturing sector outside this sector (+0.7%) indicates that the recovery is not yet generalized to all traditional sectors. The decline in investments in information technology and machinery, despite overall growth, suggests caution among some components of the productive base.
The SECO has integrated annual values into quarterly accounts based on the national accounts presented by the UST in August 2026 for the previous year, also updating the data for the previous biennium. This means that the current numbers reflect ordinary statistical corrections and revisions in economic flows, but do not change the central message: Switzerland is accelerating after a weak start to the year.

A solidifying economic growth indirectly supports the stability of social protection systems as well. Companies that see growth in revenues and employment tend to pay more stable contributions to corporate pension funds (LPP) and AVS funds, improving the financial health of these systems. item.title: VCP CO2 emissions: 2025 results and achievable targets
item.description: In 2025, the CO2 requirements for heavy commercial vehicles in Switzerland come into force: importers reach their targets with 20.8% of the fleet being fully electric.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - From 2025, CO2 regulations for new heavy commercial vehicles in Switzerland - Electric VCP quota: 20.8%, well above the European average - One fine among 13 major importers: 303,000 CHF goes to FOSTRA
## Key facts - **What**: CO2 emission regulations for newly registered VCP - When: 2025, first year of application - Where: Switzerland and Principality of Liechtenstein - Who: 13 major importers (fleet ≥5 vehicles) + small importers - VCP registered: approximately 6,300 in Switzerland, 30 in Liechtenstein (2,000 under regulations) - Electric VCP quota: 20.8% of newly registered fleet - Total fines: approximately 303,000 CHF (1 importer out of 13)
Berne, September 3, 2026 — The Swiss Federal Administration has published the first results of the application of CO2 emission regulations for new heavy commercial vehicles (VCP). The balance is encouraging: in 2025, importers achieved the vast majority of their environmental targets, thus containing the total fines to approximately 303,000 francs. A result that reflects the commitment of the transport sector towards sustainable mobility and a much higher quota of fully electric vehicles compared to the European average.
In 2025, approximately 6,300 heavy commercial vehicles were registered for the first time in Switzerland, of which approximately 2,000 fall within the scope of the new CO2 emission regulations. In the Principality of Liechtenstein, VCP registrations amounted to around 30 vehicles. Among the importers, 13 large operators (with a fleet of at least five vehicles) brought approximately 1,950 vehicles to market, while around fifty small importers distributed the remaining ones. This fragmented segment illustrates how the Swiss VCP market remains concentrated on a limited number of large players, who ensure more agile regulatory compliance.
### The Swiss push towards electric
What is positively surprising is the very high penetration of fully electric vehicles: approximately one in five newly registered VCP (20.8%) was fully electric in 2025. This is a percentage well above the European average, a sign that Switzerland is at the forefront of the transition to zero-emission fleets. This technological push has allowed several importers to remain well below the threshold represented by their average CO2 emission targets. Of the 13 major importers, only one failed to meet the set target and therefore paid a fine. The total amount of this fine is approximately 303,000 francs, a figure that goes to the National Roads and Agglomeration Traffic Fund (FOSTRA), used to finance transport infrastructure and sustainable mobility interventions in Swiss infrastructure.
The containment of fines is the direct result of importers' ability to quickly adapt to regulations that rewarded technological innovation. The vast majority of companies anticipated the transition to more efficient and, where possible, fully electric vehicles, turning a regulatory constraint into a competitive advantage in the European market. ## The impact on the competitiveness of Swiss logistics The CO2 emission regulations for VCP represent a strategic challenge for the entire logistics and freight transport ecosystem in Switzerland. Unlike in other European countries, where vehicle manufacturers have had more time to adapt, Swiss importers have moved quickly, driven by both regulations and the increasing availability of battery-powered technological solutions. This ability to adapt is crucial to maintaining Switzerland's international competitiveness as a logistics and transit hub in the heart of Europe. Transport companies operating in Switzerland face different operational costs depending on their fleet. Fully electric vehicles, although having a higher purchase cost compared to traditional internal combustion engines, offer significant savings in fuel and maintenance costs in the long term. This economic element is not marginal: a company investing in an electric fleet reduces annual operating costs, which translates into more competitive transport prices and potentially wider margins. The reduction in operating costs for those choosing sustainable vehicles represents a natural incentive that goes beyond mere regulatory compliance. ### How regulations reshape the supply chain The regulations do not only concern importers but indirectly affect the entire ecosystem. Major logistics operators purchasing VCP from the 13 main importers benefit from a greater availability of efficient and sustainable models. At the same time, regulatory pressure encourages international commercial vehicle manufacturers to develop and offer zero or low-emission models, accelerating global innovation. Switzerland, with its ambitious regulations and concrete results by 2025, becomes a pilot market for clean technologies that then spread to other European countries. The issue of costs, however, remains central. Even if a transport company benefits economically from the adoption of electric VCP in the medium to long term, the initial investment is significant and requires access to favorable credit. Federal regulations do not include direct subsidies to transporters; however, the containment of fines (only 303,000 CHF in total for the entire sector in 2025) demonstrates that the market can self-regulate when regulatory incentives are well calibrated. [Discover how environmental regulations impact corporate strategy](nav:companies) and sustainable compliance opportunities for transport companies.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## How the control and sanction system works
The control mechanism for CO2 prescriptions for VCP is structured around two pillars: monitoring new registrations and calculating the weighted average of emissions for each importer. Each importer must maintain an average CO2 emission below a specific target, determined based on the average mass of vehicles introduced to the market. This system, known as the average approach, allows flexibility: those who introduce highly efficient vehicles and various electric models can compensate for any vehicles with slightly higher emissions, as long as the average remains within the set limit.
In the first year of application (2025), out of 13 major importers, only one did not stay below the set target. This importer had to pay a penalty proportional to the target exceeded. The total amount of penalties, approximately 303,000 francs, was fully paid into the National Roads and Agglomeration Traffic Fund (FOSTRA). The same mechanism applies to penalties for cars and light commercial vehicles, creating a coherent system of public funding for mobility and transport infrastructure at the national level.
### The role of FOSTRA and the use of funds
FOSTRA represents the most direct fiscal-environmental recycling mechanism in Switzerland: the proceeds from environmental non-compliance penalties are reinvested in transport infrastructure and projects that reduce congestion and improve regional and national mobility. In 2025, the first year of application, the amount contributed was modest (303,000 CHF), both because the market adapted effectively and because the share of electric VCP exceeded expectations. If this trend continues, it is likely that the proceeds will remain contained, a sign that the regulation is positively incentivizing the sector's behavior towards sustainability.
For transport companies that purchase VCP from these importers, the message is clear: compliance with CO2 prescriptions is guaranteed if they choose suppliers operating within the Swiss regulatory framework. Any VCP registered in Switzerland from 2025 onwards from a regular importer complies ipso facto with federal prescriptions. No additional company-level control is necessary; the responsibility for compliance lies entirely with the grantor (the importer). item.title: Family allowances in the canton of Lucerne: an application guide
item.description: How do family allowances work in the Canton of Lucerne? Learn about the claim process and the role of clearinghouses.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Family allowances support families in the Canton of Lucerne. - Eligibility for allowances depends on criteria defined at the cantonal level. - The procedure requires the submission of specific documentation to the compensation fund. - The amounts vary according to the current regulations in the Canton.
## Key facts - **What**: Family and education allowances - Where: Canton of Lucerne - Who: Competent compensation fund - Amount: Variable according to cantonal legislation
Family benefits in the Canton of Lucerne represent a fundamental pillar of the local social protection system. Family and education allowances are designed to contribute to the costs associated with the maintenance and education of children. The provision of such contributions is managed through compensation funds, which operate in accordance with the legislation applicable in the Lucerne territory. To access these benefits, beneficiaries must meet specific criteria, which are verified by the competent authorities during the application analysis phase. The structure of the system aims to ensure structured support for parents, ensuring that resources are distributed consistently with the purposes set out in the local regulatory framework.
### Management of benefits The competence for the provision of allowances lies with the compensation funds active in the Canton. These institutions play a crucial role in assessing entitlements, acting as the main point of contact for applicants. The verification process is based on an analysis of the family and work situation, ensuring that each case is handled in accordance with the current provisions. It is essential that the interested party contacts their reference fund to obtain detailed information about their entitlements, avoiding reliance on general or outdated estimates of the most recent cantonal directives. Transparency in the relationship between the providing entity and the beneficiary is ensured by standardized administrative procedures, which protect the right of each family to receive what is due based on their profile. The analysis of dynamics related to family allowances requires a clear understanding of how the social security system works in Switzerland. While the general bases are established at the federal level, the concrete application and the amount of payments can differ significantly depending on the Canton of belonging. In the specific case of Lucerne, the local regulations define the parameters within which the compensation funds operate. This means that, unlike other social contributions that follow a uniform national logic, family allowances reflect the specific policies adopted by the Lucerne authorities to support the cost of living for resident families.

The procedure for requesting family allowances in the Canton of Lucerne follows a consolidated protocol that every applicant must observe precisely. The first step is to identify the compensation fund with which the employer is affiliated, or, in the case of self-employed workers, the one to which one is personally registered. The application must be completed using the official forms provided by the institution, ensuring that all required documentation to prove entitlement to the allowance is attached. The completeness of the data provided is the determining factor for the speed of processing by the offices.
### Operational steps Once the request is submitted, the compensation fund proceeds with the investigation, verifying the existence of the necessary requirements. At this stage, it is essential to respond promptly to any requests for clarification or additional documentation that may be received from the offices. Precision in communication is key to avoiding delays. After approval, the allowances are paid according to the agreed methods, usually via bank transfer, ensuring a constant flow of resources for the family unit. item.title: AVS and supplementary benefits: contribution gaps
item.description: How the first pillar works in the Swiss system: calculation of the AVS pension, contribution gaps, cantonal compensation fund and supplementary benefits for the minimum living wage.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - AVS is the first pillar of the Swiss social security system: pension calculated on years of contributions - Contribution gaps (years without payments) reduce the monthly pension amount - Supplementary benefits intervene when AVS does not cover the minimum living standard - Cantonal compensation fund manages the system at the local level
## Key facts - **What**: Three-pillar pension system (mandatory AVS, professional LPP, private third pillar) - Contributions: 5.3% employee + 5.3% employer (10.6% total on salary); self-employed pay both shares - Management: UFAS oversees at the federal level; cantonal compensation funds manage operationally - Minimum living standard: Amount set by cantons to ensure dignity in retirement - Right: At least 1 year of contributions to access AVS pension
The first pillar of the Swiss social security system rests on AVS (Old-Age and Survivors' Insurance), a mandatory contributory system managed through cantonal compensation funds. Each canton has its own fund — a public body that collects contributions, maintains individual accounts, calculates pensions, and pays them out monthly for the beneficiary's lifetime.
The AVS pension is not uniform: it depends on the number of years of contributions paid and the average amount of salaries declared during the working career. Those who accumulate contribution gaps — periods in which payment was absent, reduced, or interrupted — receive a lower pension compared to those with a complete contribution career. These gaps are the main factor in reducing the benefit in the first pillar.
### How the AVS pension is calculated
The cantonal compensation fund calculates the pension based on the arithmetic average of the incomes subject to contribution during ALL years from the first payment to retirement age (65 for men, 64 for women). If there are 5 missing years in a 40-year career (due to unemployment, inactivity, employment gaps), the overall average decreases, even if the 35 years of actual work had high incomes. This mechanism protects the redistributive system of AVS but penalizes those with a fragmented career.
Contributors pay 5.3% of gross salary, employers pay 5.3% (total 10.6%); self-employed pay both shares on their declared professional income. Contributions are mandatory from the first day of work and continue until retirement age. The taxable base follows the cantonal legislation of each territory, but the contribution distribution is identical throughout Switzerland. ### Complementary services: the role of the State when AVS is not enough
When the AVS pension — calculated on actual contributions — does not reach the level of the minimum living allowance set by the cantonal authorities, supplementary benefits intervene. These are not the result of a new contribution: they are tax transfers, financed by general taxation (direct federal, cantonal, municipal tax, VAT). Their purpose is to guarantee a minimum standard of living to the elderly and disabled who, due to circumstances of their work biography, cannot count on a full AVS income.
The supplementary benefits cover the gap between the income received and the certified cost of living (rent, essential services, basic necessities). Each canton sets its own living minimum and access criteria; each municipality applies the cantonal criteria to its territory. The disparity between cantons and municipalities is significant: the living minimum in Geneva can differ significantly from that in a mountain canton, reflecting different living costs.
Who is eligible? Conditions vary, but generally access is granted to those who receive an AVS or disability (AI) pension below the local minimum, have capital resources within cantonal thresholds and reside permanently in the canton/municipality. Complementary services are NOT generic assistance: they are a legal right for those who meet objective criteria.

## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Check your own contribution career: concrete procedures
The first step is to contact the cantonal compensation fund of your canton of residence. You can do this: - Via the official website of the fund (almost all cantons allow online requests) - By mail, sending a request form - In person at the local office of the fund
Request a free extract of your AVS contribution career. The document will arrive within 2-4 weeks and will contain: - A year-by-year list of declared incomes - Confirmation of paid contributions - Explicit identification of gaps - Calculation base for the estimate of future pension
Take the time to carefully check each line. Verify that: - All work periods are recorded (compare with your memory of employers) - Salary amounts match your pay slips - There are no erroneous gaps (years that should be covered but are not) - Years of work in other cantons or abroad have not been omitted (if applicable)
If you find discrepancies, report them to the fund within 30 days: it is obliged to investigate and correct the official data. After this period, corrections are more difficult and require lengthy administrative procedures.
### Buying back gaps and entitlement to supplementary benefits
If you discover gaps, ask the fund if you can buy them back. Buying back AVS is optional for some periods (training, unemployment): it consists of paying a lump sum to the fund, which recognizes those years as 'covered' for the calculation of the pension. The cost varies depending on the years to be bought back and the declared incomes, but it can be significant (hundreds to thousands of francs). The fund will calculate the permanent monthly pension increase that would result from it, allowing you to evaluate whether it is economically worthwhile (how much the buy-back will cost vs. how much the pension will increase over time).
If you do not buy back, or if the buy-back is impossible for some periods, check with the municipality of residence if you will be entitled to supplementary benefits once retired. The municipality has an office (social services, personal services) that: - Calculates the local minimum living standard - Evaluates your resources (property, real estate, income) - Decides the monthly amount of the benefit - Approves or denies the formal application
### Concrete actions: checklist for preparation
1. **Request the extract today**: Do not wait until retirement. If you are over 50, it is urgent. 2. Check and correct: Verify the work years and amounts within 30 days. 3. Evaluate the buy-back: Ask the fund for the cost and benefit of buying back critical gaps. 4. Inform yourself about supplementary benefits: Contact your municipality at least 6 months before retirement age. 5. Estimate your pension: Use the [online AVS calculator](nav:pension) for an initial projection, then verify the exact numbers of your situation with the fund.
Our [pension calculation tool](nav:pension) helps you estimate the monthly value of your AVS based on known data; however, for certainty, you must consult the cantonal compensation fund directly with your official data.
